1:
The title takes three of them in different directions. Augustine of Hippo works on a form of the inscription that says the hymns of David the son of Jesse have failed, observing that nowhere else is the father’s name added, and that a hymn must have three things, praise, praise of God, and singing, so that a failure of hymns is a painful thing to report. Adam Clarke takes the heading as an ascription to the singer whose name it bears, places him under the captivity, and makes the psalm a consolation for a people in bondage who saw a nation far more corrupt than themselves prospering and holding them down. Keil and Delitzsch place it in its collection, the first of a group of eleven and the counterpart of an earlier psalm; the temptation in it, they say against one scholar, is not toward heathenism but toward free-thinking, and its doubts about the moral order are set at rest as they are in two other psalms and in the book of Job.

On the opening word the readings diverge by a hair. C.H. Spurgeon renders it not truly but only: God is only good to his covenanted ones, nothing else but good, beyond dispute and without mixture. Charles Ellicott makes the particle a rejoinder to something supposed, like the Latin word it answers to, and quotes an English poet whose lines run that surely the gods are good and one would fain think so, but that virtue in distress and vice in triumph make atheists of mankind. He asks whether the second clause limits the first or merely repeats it, and holds that the subject requires a limitation, since a moral correspondence with their profession is necessary even in the chosen people. John Gill allows both senses, the nation literally and the Israel God has chosen and called; John Wesley keeps to the true Israelites who serve him in spirit and truth.

Matthew Henry attends to the abrupt beginning and reads the verse as a man checking himself: he had been thinking of the prosperity of the wicked, and while he mused the fire burned. What follows he takes as the principle the writer resolved to hold to while parleying with the temptation, and sets it beside three others: one sufferer fixed on the omniscience of God, that times are not hidden from the Almighty; a prophet on his justice, that he is righteous even when we plead with him; another on his holiness, that he is of purer eyes than to behold iniquity; and this psalmist on his goodness. John Calvin gives the argument of the whole psalm in four movements: the writer extols the righteousness of God, confesses the shock of seeing the wicked abound while the children of God pine away and God seems to sit in heaven idle, a shock almost disposing him to cast off all concern about religion, reproves his own folly in judging rashly from the present state of things, and concludes that we must leave providence to take its course by the degrees determined in the secret purpose of God.

At the slipping feet the metaphor is pressed. Ellicott notes that the word means literally poured out, an obvious figure for instability, and quotes a Latin poet on limbs that dissolve and flow. Spurgeon opens the narrative as a battle hard fought, in which the half-defeated became in the end wholly victorious, and marks the connection between the heart and the feet, since when men doubt the righteousness of God their own integrity begins to waver. Clarke states plainly what was at stake, that he had nearly given up his confidence and was ready to think the Judge of all the earth did not do right; Wesley says his faith in providence was almost overthrown, and Gill hears an ungrateful creature confessing after a thousand kindnesses.
3:
The envy is defined before it is described. Charles Ellicott corrects the word for the foolish to the arrogant, and suggests that the verb rendered saw is here synonymous with envied, as the Latin word for envy also carries the sense of looking. John Gill identifies them from a Jewish writer as the atheists who deny the creation, wise in things natural and without understanding in things spiritual. Adam Clarke answers with a heathen maxim and then with an argument: the ancients said that the prosperity of the wicked is a reproach to the gods, but they had no just conception of future rewards and punishments; and besides, man could not bear prosperity, for if men had uninterrupted comforts here perhaps not one soul would seek a preparation for heaven, so that the warfare of human life is the highest proof of a providence as benevolent as it is wise.

The fourth verse defeats them, and one says so. Ellicott calls the English quite unintelligible and no fair rendering of the Hebrew, which gives that there are no bands to their death; the word might by a Latin analogy mean pangs, so that they have a painless death, but that would be out of keeping with the psalm, and the versions give no help, so that emendation is absolutely necessary. He reports an ingenious conjecture which by the change of one letter yields that there are no bands to their yoke, making them chartered libertines, which agrees with the animal grossness of the clause that follows. Keil and Delitzsch work on a different variant, favoured by three scholars and by the Greek, in which the iniquity of such men presses forth out of a fat heart, granting that the parallelism decides for it. John Wesley keeps the received text and makes the bands judicial, since such men are not dragged to death by the magistrate as they deserve. Gill offers two renderings, no bands in their death or none until their death, and notes a version in which they pay their death no regard at all. Clarke turns it into contrast: many of the godly have sore conflicts at their end, their enemy thrusting at them that their confidence may be shaken, but of this the ungodly know nothing, since Satan will not molest men of whom he is sure; they die without a sigh, and so go off as quiet as a lamb to the slaughter.

The pride worn as a chain is dressed three ways. Gill takes the figure for bondage, since those under the power of pride are its slaves, chained by it, though they bind it about themselves fancying it an ornament; and he traces the sin from the devils and the first parents to Sodom, where fulness of bread and pride went together. Clarke sees an allusion to office, since chains of gold and rings were the ensigns of magistracy, so that violence encompassed these men as their chains encompassed their necks; and he notes a version that turns the chain into a diadem formed out of the plunder of the defenceless. Ellicott renders the couplet that pride is their necklace and violence their mantle, the first figure coming either from the sums the rich lavished on jewellery or from the usual description of the proud as stiffnecked.

At the eyes standing out with fatness Clarke is bluntest and then most careful. He quotes a version in which the countenance is changed because of fatness, and observes that corpulency obliterates the natural lines of the face, so that little remains beside the human hog. Then he doubts the English of the second clause, that they have more than heart could wish, asking whose heart ever said it had enough that had not its portion in God; it would be more literal, he says, to render that they surpass the thoughts of their own heart.
9:
The mouth set against the heavens is turned by one of them into a picture. Charles Ellicott renders the preposition in rather than against, so that they have set their mouth in the heavens while their tongue walks through the earth, an image of towering pride vaunting itself to the skies and trumpeting its own praises through the world. John Gill takes the heavens for God and lists what such men speak against, his being, perfections, decrees and providence, and reports two other readings, a Jewish interpreter who understands the angels and a version that understands the saints, adding that the words may be applied to civil magistrates. Adam Clarke enumerates the acts: they blaspheme God, ridicule religion, mock at providence and laugh at a future state, traducing the memory of the just and criticizing every dispensation of God. John Wesley keeps the walking tongue to a liberty that reproaches all sorts of persons.

The tenth verse is the crux of the psalm, and Clarke says so in the strongest terms in this chapter. There are very few verses in the Bible, he writes, that have been more variously translated, and like the man in the fable the translators have blown the hot to cool it and the cold to warm it; he then sets out four renderings: that the people of God fall off to such men and reap no small advantage by it; that if they came before them they would be squeezed until the juice was wrung out of their bodies; that a version turns the clause against the people of the Lord, bruised with mallets so that they pour out abundance of tears; and that a Latin version has the people returning and days of abundance following. Ellicott prefers the reading of an old English prayer book, resting on the Hebrew margin, which describes the popularity such self-applause gains, the people turning to these men and a cup of adulation being sucked out by them. Gill offers three constructions of his own, the people of God returning to the same temptation as the psalmist, professors returning to the company of such men, or the followers of the wicked returning to their leaders; Wesley takes the last and has them partaking of the same prosperity.

At the question how God knows, the difficulty is whose question it is. Clarke gives both possibilities: either the people, stumbled at the prosperity of the wicked, are ready to say that God cannot know these things or he would never dispense his favours so; or the words belong to the wicked, who reckon that they may oppress and live as they list and God knows nothing of it. Gill removes a misunderstanding first, that the question is not about the manner of God’s knowing, since he knows not by sense or reasoning but beholds all things in his own eternal mind; the question is about his knowledge itself.

The summary that follows is where the doubt turns dangerous. Keil and Delitzsch say plainly that for such men doubt becomes the transition to apostasy, and that the poet has resolved the riddle of the unequal distribution of men’s fortunes in a wholly different way; at the following verse they refuse two proposed emendations, one adopted against the accents by an early authority, since prepositions are sometimes used elliptically and the text needs no mending. Gill draws the line the psalm draws, that these men prosper in worldly things but not in their souls, having their good things here and their evil things to come, at ease and undistressed by their own sins. Clarke and Wesley keep to the plainest sense of the complaint that follows, that the writer had cleansed his heart to no purpose and been plagued all the day long.
15:
The turn of the psalm begins with something not said. Matthew Henry counts it the first point gained in the victory, that respect for the people of God restrained the writer from uttering the thought he had conceived; though he thought amiss he took care not to speak it. C.H. Spurgeon makes it a rule: it is not always wise to speak one’s thoughts, for kept within they injure only ourselves, but once uttered their mischief may be great, and from such a man the utterance would have been a heavy blow to the whole brotherhood; he paused instead, and in his case second thoughts were by far the best. Charles Ellicott renders the clause with two finite verbs for one thought, as the Hebrew often does: if, thought I, I should reason thus, I should be faithless to the generation of thy sons. Adam Clarke puts it as a discovery, that the writer had reasoned incorrectly and had against him the uniform testimony of all the children of God, who from generation to generation have testified that the Judge of all the earth does right. John Wesley defines the offence as grieving and discouraging them and tempting them to revolt.

The attempt to think it out is admitted to have failed. John Gill says the reconciling was attempted by the mere dint of reason, without consulting the sacred oracles or experience. Ellicott glosses the verb as reflecting in order to know, trying to get to the bottom of the matter. Clarke fills the failure with history, that on reviewing the story of their fathers he saw God had never utterly abandoned them and that it was unreasonable to think he would now do what he had never done; and yet, he adds, the continuance of the captivity puzzles him again. Keil and Delitzsch mark the change of standpoint, that the poet calms himself with the solution that has come to him and places himself at the standpoint of the end.

Where the solution came is the question of the chapter, and Clarke raises an objection against his own dating. If the psalm was written during the captivity, as he thinks there is little room to doubt, how can its writer speak of going into the sanctuary, when there was none in the land of exile and the one at home had long been destroyed? Gill takes the sanctuary plainly, the house where the word was read and prayer made, and draws the lesson that the temptation never so far prevailed as to make the man neglect public worship, which is the very means of relief under doubts; some, he notes, understand by it the Scriptures themselves. Wesley takes it of the practice of those times, of resorting in difficult cases to the sanctuary and the oracle there. Ellicott makes it the service itself, where the blessings on righteousness and the warnings against wickedness, read from the law or chanted from some ancient song, gave the needed turn to the writer’s speculations; he began to think not of the advantages of sin but of its consequences, though still, Ellicott adds, of consequences in this world, the thought of a hereafter not having established itself sufficiently to have an ethical force.

What was understood there is set out briefly. Keil and Delitzsch describe the vision of the end, that the ungodly come to terrible destruction in a moment, and note that it would be beneath the poet’s dignity to let himself be tempted further by doubting thoughts. Clarke states the same conclusion as a discovery, that the unequal distribution of good and evil argues a future judgment, that the present is a state of trial, and that the prosperity of the wicked here was a prelude to their destruction. Gill and Wesley keep to the shortness of that prosperity, and Spurgeon to the suddenness of the fall.
21:
The confession of folly is where the psalm turns generous, and Matthew Henry says why. He calls it an old riddle unriddled again, meat coming out of the eater and sweetness out of the strong, since the writer made a good improvement of the temptation that had almost overcome him; a man who stumbles and does not fall, he adds, takes the longer steps forward for recovering himself, and God would not suffer his people to be tempted if his grace were not sufficient to make them gainers by it.

The word for the grieved heart is worked over by four of them. Charles Ellicott gives it literally, that the heart grew sour, or as we say was soured. John Gill reports the word as meaning leavened, so that the man was in a ferment, as a Latin playwright uses the phrase of one in anger; others, he says, render it inflamed, not with the love of God but with wrath. C.H. Spurgeon follows a reading that his heart was soured and makes a diagnosis of it: the man had become melancholy and choleric, had poisoned his own life at the fountain-head and made all its streams bitter, and his hard thoughts were like so many stones in his kidneys, so that he was wretched through his own reflections. John Wesley keeps it to being deeply wounded with disquieting thoughts. Adam Clarke takes the next verse of himself, that he felt as if he were a beast in stupidity, having let his mind be occupied with sensible things like the beasts that perish; Ellicott corrects the English word there from foolish to brutish.

What follows the confession is read as the answer to it. Gill takes the continual presence two ways, that the man was not suffered to depart finally, and that the words may be rendered as a promise for hereafter, since the saints are always in union with the Lord though not always in communion. Clarke turns it to his people as well as himself, that they are under a guardian care and upheld continually, and while in that right hand shall not be utterly cast down. On the guidance Gill offers three renderings, with thy counsel, according to thy counsel, meaning the determinate purposes of God, and by thy counsel, meaning the Scriptures and the Spirit who is a spirit of counsel. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the sequence of the thought, which has now passed from the standpoint of the end to the possession of God himself.

The last verse of this section is the one they all admire. Clarke says the original is more emphatic than the English, which asks who is there to me in the heavens and adds that with thee I have desired nothing in the earth; and he sets a condition on it, that no man can say this who has not taken God for his portion in reference to both worlds. Ellicott renders the second clause that besides thee I have no delight on earth. Spurgeon marks the turn of the whole psalm here, that the man turns from the glitter which had fascinated him to the true gold which was his real treasure, having found his God better than all the wealth and honour he had envied, and more excellent than all in heaven; henceforth his wishes should no longer ramble. Gill fills out the heaven that is emptied by the question, excluding the sun and moon and stars in the lower heavens from worship and trust, and the angels and glorified saints in the highest, and notes that the words may also be rendered as asking who is on my side in heaven.
26:
The failing of flesh and heart is read as death approaching. John Gill canvasses four occasions for the failing, vehement desire of communion deferred, afflictive dispensations, inward trials and desertions, and last what he prefers, a body emaciated by sickness and a heart failing at the point of death, since the heart, as the philosophers say, is the first that lives and the last that dies. Adam Clarke makes it simply the prospect of dying, when even natural courage will fail and nothing but supernatural support will be available; he renders the answering clause literally as the rock of my heart, and takes the portion as an allusion to the dividing of the land, so that the writer asks no inheritance below but looks for one above, since nothing but God can content the desires of an immortal spirit, and even that would not satisfy without the prospect of its being for ever.

At the perishing of those who are far from God, Clarke turns from exposition to controversy. The word perish, he says, is generally used to mean coming to nothing, and some apply it so to the finally impenitent, that they shall be annihilated; but he asks where that is to be found in the Scriptures and answers, in no part properly understood, since in the new heavens and the new earth none of the wicked shall be found, and yet the wicked shall be in their own place. To suppose them annihilated he calls as great a heresy, though scarcely so absurd, as to hold that the pains of the lost are corrective and that the fire shall burn out; and he adds the argument that if punishment is not eternal there is presumptive evidence that glory will not be eternal either. John Wesley keeps to the figure of the verse instead, that those who revolt to work wickedness are said in Scripture to go a whoring. Gill defines the distance as being alienated from the life of God, far from his law and from righteousness whether moral or evangelical.

The last verse is the writer’s own conclusion, and each takes something different from it. Gill hears in it a recent experience rather than a maxim, since the man had lately been delivered out of a sore temptation in the very place he now commends; and he divides the good three ways, an honourable good, becoming and commendable, a pleasant good that yields delight, and a profitable good, adding that when the drawing near is done aright it is with faith, sincerity, reverence and a holy boldness. Clarke sets the verse against the one before it, since those who are far off shall perish and therefore it is ill for them, while those who draw near shall be saved and therefore it is good for them; he explains the declaring of the works as testifying to all how good it is to draw near and what a sufficient portion God is to the soul of man; and he reports that four versions add a clause about the gates of the daughter of Sion, which he thinks makes a better finish, though no Hebrew copy acknowledges it. Charles Ellicott corrects the sense of the works, which are not God’s doings but the works prescribed to the writer, the messages entrusted to him, and here no doubt the conclusions he had reached and the truths revealed to him, in contrast with the false opinions from which he had been freed. Keil and Delitzsch give the verse without comment, printing the text alone where the others expound.
